Native Language Identification
            (NLI) aims at identifying the
            native
            languages of authors by analyzing their text samples written in a
            non-native
            language. Most existing studies investigate this task for educational applications such as
            second language acquisition
            and require the learner corpora. This article performs NLI in a challenging context of the
            user-generated-content
            (UGC) where authors are fluent and advanced non-native speakers of a second language. Existing NLI studies with UGC (i) rely on the content-specific/social-network features and may not be generalizable to other domains and datasets, (ii) are unable to capture the variations of the language-usage-patterns within a text sample, and (iii) are not associated with any outlier handling mechanism. Moreover, since there is a sizable number of people who have acquired non-English second languages due to the economic and immigration policies, there is a need to gauge the applicability of NLI with UGC to other languages. Unlike existing solutions, we define a topic-independent feature space, which makes our solution generalizable to other domains and datasets. Based on our feature space, we present a solution that mitigates the effect of outliers in the data and helps capture the variations of the language-usage-patterns within a text sample. Specifically, we represent each text sample as a
            point set
            and identify the top-
            k
            stylistically similar text samples (SSTs) from the corpus. We then apply the
            
              probabilistic
              k
              nearest neighbors’
            
            classifier on the identified top-
            k
            SSTs to predict the native languages of the authors. To conduct experiments, we create three new corpora where each corpus is written in a different language, namely,
            English, French
            , and
            German
            . Our experimental studies show that our solution outperforms competitive methods and reports more than 80% accuracy across languages.

result.paraphrase: Native Language Identification (NLI) seeks to determine authors’ native languages by examining text samples they have written in a non-native language. Most prior work studies this problem for educational settings such as second language acquisition and depends on learner corpora. In this article, we address NLI in the more difficult setting of user-generated content (UGC), where authors are fluent, advanced non-native speakers of a second language. Existing UGC-based NLI studies (i) depend on content-specific or social-network features and may not generalize across domains and datasets, (ii) cannot model variations in language-usage patterns within a text sample, and (iii) lack any mechanism for handling outliers. In addition, because many people have learned non-English second languages due to economic and immigration policies, it is important to assess whether NLI with UGC also applies to other languages. Rather than using existing approaches, we define a topic-independent feature space that improves generalizability to other domains and datasets. On the basis of this feature space, we propose a method that reduces the impact of outliers and captures variations in language-use patterns within a sample. In particular, each text sample is represented as a point set, and the top-k stylistically similar text samples (SSTs) are retrieved from the corpus. A probabilistic k nearest neighbors classifier is then applied to these top-k SSTs to predict the authors’ native languages. For evaluation, we construct three new corpora, each written in a different language: English, French, and German. Our experiments show that the proposed solution outperforms competitive methods and achieves over 80% accuracy across languages.
